title: Meeting room booking capstone
idea: The capstone is one system, a Meeting Room Booking System, that you take from a written brief to tested, documented Java you can defend in a review.
points: Employees search free rooms by capacity, book a slot, and cancel their own bookings.
Agree scope first: list must-haves, name what is out, write each as a check.
Start with a walking skeleton: the thinnest slice that books rooms end to end.
Each later page replaces one shortcut in the skeleton with a production-grade module.

items.label: Requirements
items.text: Turn the brief into use cases, actors and entities. Agree what is out.

items.label: Class diagram
items.text: Draw `BookingService`, the repositories and the extension points as interfaces before any logic.

items.label: Core modules
items.text: Build entities and repositories first, then the service that enforces the booking rules.

items.label: Errors and monitoring
items.text: Replace returned strings with `BookingException` subclasses, structured logs and counters.

items.label: Patterns and tests
items.text: Make `ConflictPolicy` a Strategy and `BookingListener` an Observer, then cover the rules with checks.

items.label: Review and present
items.text: Collect peer feedback, refine, document with UML, and explain every trade-off you made.

code.title: Walking skeleton
code.caption: Day one: the smallest program that books rooms and rejects a clash. Shortcuts are deliberate and marked.

walk.text: `Booking` is a record. Hours are `double`, so 9.5 means 09:30. An empty slot is rejected at birth.
Two slots overlap when each starts before the other ends. Equal end and start do not overlap.
The comment names the shortcuts: one class, one list, strings instead of exceptions. Later pages remove each.
`book` builds a candidate and scans existing bookings. The first clash wins and names the blocker.
Returning a string is a skeleton shortcut. c11-t04 throws `RoomTakenException` instead; c11-t05 handles it.
The run shows a clash, a back-to-back slot, and the same hours in another room.

code.title: Scope as checks
code.caption: Each requirement becomes a named check. Unbuilt ones are listed as TODO, so scope is visible in one run.

walk.text: Every must-have rule is one line that reads like the brief: a name plus a boolean.
Requirements not built yet stay on the list as TODO. Nothing in scope is forgotten silently.
A hand-written `check` runner stands in for JUnit 5, which this book cannot run.
`SlotBook` keeps slots per room in a `TreeMap`, so any printing order is stable.
The same overlap rule as the skeleton. Back-to-back slots pass because the comparison is strict.
The summary line is your progress bar for the whole capstone.

pitfalls: Coding before agreeing scope: you build recurring meetings nobody asked for and miss cancellation.
Starting with a perfect domain model instead of an end-to-end slice delays your first working run.
Leaving skeleton shortcuts unmarked; reviewers later mistake them for design decisions.

quiz.q: Using the skeleton, what does the second call print?
options: IllegalArgumentException: start must be before end
quiz.why: Overlap needs `start < other.end`; 10.0 is not below 10.0, so the slots only touch. The list holds one booking, so the id is B2.

takeaway: Agree scope as checks, then grow one walking skeleton into the system.

starters: How do I decide what is out of scope in a 45-minute interview?
Why use double for hours instead of LocalTime?
